Thoughts on Chinua Achebe's "Things Fall Apart"?  Just finished it and I don't exactly know how to feel. This is going to be super informal and written in a rush, so sorry if I don't make much sense or leave ideas unfinished.The book spent part one just sort of rambling and going on about how terrible Okonkwo is, but how his bad qualities come from a place of fear. He then gets exiled, leading us into part two. Small things happen in part two. It seems like it's trying to be a series of small things that chip away at Okonkwo's hard shell until he returns home and, seeing how alien his tribe has become while he was gone, he breaks. Part three is just sorta. There. And then in one paragraph he kills someone, not much build up even though it should be something big. And then three or four paragraphs later they casually mention that he's killed himself. It just... Happens. Which I guess you could say is supposed to make the reader aware of how suicide feels for people, how it just happens with no warning. But, it didn't even feel like much changed, or there was any consequence. I think it's supposed to be one of those endings that is supposed to leave you feeling unsatisfied because that's how the situation is supposed to feel for everyone involved, including the reader. However, it's executed so poorly that it's not not satisfying, it's just. Over. No real finality. My mind keeps being dragged back to 1984 due to similarities, which I get it's sorta unfair to compare Things Fall Apart to 1984, but that's how a lot of people talk about it. Let's start with the beginning.The first sentence or so of a story generally has a lot of importance to how the story is going to be told and what the focus of that story is going to be.So, the first sentence of Things Fall Apart focuses on character (Okonkwo), stating that the story is going to be about and focused on character. 1984 starts with setting because that's what the story is about, the characters are just vessels for the reader to experience this world through. So, you'd expect Things Fall Apart to be primarily focused on characters and the style of conveying information to correlate with this type of story, but... it's not. The entire book reads like a nonfiction book, just stating things, save for a few parts and a few admittedly eloquently written lines ("Living fire begets cold, impotent ash."). How does the author make up for this? Got me. I have no clue. It seems like you would make up for that by having things actually happen, but nothing really does happen, and when things do happen, they occur within the space of a few paragraphs until it's over. Then it's just back to waiting until something interesting happens. There's a difference between taking a long time to build your character and nothing happening. Things Fall Apart falls into the latter category.Let's go to the end now. In Things Fall Apart, Okonkwo's hard shell of masculinity, partly pushed on him by his culture and partly (mostly) pushed on him by himself and his fear, shatters. He kills an English man. This  be a big deal, but, as everything else in this book, it's over and done with within the next paragraph. In the next chapter, some men are looking for him, and Obierika points them towards a tree where Okonkwo has hanged himself. I think that this is supposed to be surprising (there must be a reason the point of view shifts from inside Okonkwo's head to someone else's), and I mean, I guess it was, just not in the right way. It should've been like, "Wow, he's dead." Not, "Oh, okay. Guess the book is over now." An ending should have a purpose, and deepen the connection the reader's mind has with the focus of the story, but this one doesn't. In 1984, the ending has a purpose besides ending the book. It entrenches you further in the world (the main focal point of the book). It drives home the point to the book, which Things Fall Apart does as well. But, in this one, it has significance. Let me explain.Both Things Fall Apart and 1984 are trying to, in one way or another, drive home how small the characters are to the antagonists (the English and Ingsoc/the world as a whole, respectively). In 1984, O'Brien, representing how wrong and alien the world of 1984 is, has this huge, sprawling monologue, which is then followed by a skip in time to Winston and Julia becoming passive. This excellently shows how powerful the antagonist is and how hopeless the situation is. In Things Fall Apart, Okonkwo kills himself, and within the next two or three paragraphs the white man makes a remark about how he might make the story of Okonkwo a mere sentence in his book he's writing (possibly mirroring how brief Achebe makes everything that happens in the book last?). Now, out of context, both seem to be going after the same thing in similar ways, just small changes in execution. But, one is more effective than the other. I'm not saying that Achebe should've written a monologue like Orwell did, but something should've been done. Maybe something in between?Another thing is the character development of Okonkwo. Okonkwo doesn't really change throughout the story, and at the end his tragic flaw kills him. It almost feels like a Greek tragedy in that way. It feels like things that happen to "give him character" happen only to do just that, not because they are part of the point of the book or are important. Characterization shouldn't be the only thing in the story, there also has to be this thing called "plot". The characterization is almost completely separated from the events of the book, he just does things that he  do (because it's his character) and nothing advances the plot except when it needs to.I guess that the book was trying to emphasize that Okonkwo is a product of his culture, but it never focuses on that for very long. It seems the book doesn't know what to focus on so it focuses on nothing at all, or one thing for two seconds.I don't know. How about I stop rambling and actually open the discussion.I guess all I'm trying to say is that this book should've been called "Things Just Sort Of Happen" or "Yams and Domestic Abuse".TL;DR Things Fall Apart is all over the place, nothing happens and when it does it has no impact on the reader, severe lack of tone and common storytelling devices, etc.
